newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Stephen Koukoulas, Citibank: The A$/commodity link.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Stephen Koukoulas, Citibank: The A$/commodity link.

text.p: By Stephen Koukoulas, Senior Economist, Citibank Australia
The value of a currency is determined by many variables.

For the A$, history has shown that the main determinants have been commodity prices (because of the importance of commodities in Australia's export base) and interest rate differentials (Australia has been seen as a high yielder).
But other factors are also influential in driving currencies, with relative inflation, policy credibility, current account imbalances and sentiment all impacting from time to time.

While commodity prices and interest rate differentials will remain strong influences on the A$, there are some good reasons to think that other factors have and will continue to increase in importance.

Given these factors are likely to be positive, it suggests the A$ can mover higher in a structural sense, even without a lift in commodity prices and even if interest rate differentials remain broadly unchanged at current historically low levels.
These positive influences expected to underpin the A$ over the medium term include:
-- a diversification of the export base, with the net services balance recording increasing surpluses, plus the rapid increase in exports of manufactures

-- A re-rating of Australia from offshore on the back of the acknowledgment of the inflation credentials of the RBA, the robust fiscal settings at both the Commonwealth and state/local level and the anticipated acceleration of already progressive microeconomic reforms.
DIVERSIFICATION OF THE EXPORT BASE
In 1980, the share of exports accounted for by services was around 16 percent, with exports of manufactures around 11 percent.
Exports of agricultural and mining produce accounted for the remaining 73 percent.
By 1995, the share of exports from services had increased to 26 percent, with exports of manufactures up to 21 percent.
Exports of agricultural and mining produce had fallen to 53 percent.
As a result of these shifting shares, the services and manufacturers' terms of trade have become increasingly important in driving the A$, while commodity prices have probably started to wane.
Indeed, the strength in services exports has resulted in the net services balance moving into surplus over the past year, with the momentum firmly in place to build upon that structural change.

On the basis of Australia continuing to see increasing services exports on the back of its advantages in tourism, in particular, but also other areas such as education, health, engineering services and computer software, the trend to larger services surpluses looks promising.
If realised, the A$/commodity price link should slowly but surely diminish.
THE RE-RATING OF AUSTRALIA
Macro and micro economic policy settings are judged by the international investor community and influence their decisions on the risks of investing in particular countries.

For Australia, the policy settings have gained a large degree of credibility in recent years, aided by the RBA's success in managing an economic cycle and a half with inflation remaining in the broad 2-3 percent range.

There were a few doubters who mistakenly believed that while the previous government was in power and Mr Fraser was RBA Governor, there was a lack of independence from the RBA and/or that monetary policy settings would be compromised by political needs.

The change of government in March and the appointment of Mr Macfarlane as RBA Governor has helped to overcome these concerns via the formalisation of the inflation target. Australia is increasingly being acknowledged as a low inflation country.
Fiscal policy settings slipped with the 1990 recession and the failure of the previous government to wind back the budget deficit more quickly.

But with the substantial fiscal tightening announced in the August budget and the prospect of fiscal surpluses over the near term, the increasing policy credibility now being built in Australia is further enhanced.

Microeconomic issues are important in that the promotion of greater productivity and flexibility in the economy is seen as building international competitiveness (lowering the current account deficit) and helping to lock in low inflation.
Substantial reform in many product markets and increasingly in the labour market have built a credible microeconomic framework for Australia.
When investors weigh up these elements, the Australian fundamentals look good and are sufficiently robust to ensure strong capital inflows and, hence, probably a stronger A$.
OUTLOOK

While making point forecasts for the A$ is fraught with difficulties, the fundamental economic and policy changes suggest that the A$ could well be looking forward to trading a US$0.75 to US$0.90 broad range over the next five years, making a structural appreciation from the broad US$0.65 to US$0.80 range evident over the past decade.

And what has occurred in the last few months with the A$ maintaining a firm tone despite lower commodity prices and narrower interest differentials is evidence of the early stages of adjustment to a higher range.
On balance, from a shorter term view, the A$ could well re-test US$0.80 by end 1996, with a move to US$0.83 or a little higher achievable during 1997.
Key risks to the bullish A$ outlook are linked to either policy failure on behalf of the government or the RBA or an external shock, including possibly from a sharp dip in commodity prices.
If commoditiy prices pick up, the A$ could move even higher.
